warnings.text: Some models have disputed published output (badged below). Measured output generally matches published figures, so no derating is applied — but confirm with the manufacturer.

If you run a variable-speed pump, keep the lowest speed above roughly 14 GPM (1.5″ tee). The flow switch reacts to water velocity, so too slow a speed stops chlorine production without any obvious fault.

On install, set the cell-type setting to match the cell you actually fit — this panel works out salt from cell performance rather than a salt sensor, so a mismatch makes salt read wrong and can stop chlorine production. Confirm real salt with a K-1766 drop test rather than trusting the display.

Hold CYA at 70–80 once you are running on salt. Higher CYA shields chlorine from sunlight, so the cell makes less to hold the same FC and lasts longer. Note the output percentage is a share of pump run time — change your schedule and you will need to re-tune it.

Cell life is measured in generating hours — roughly 10,000 for OEM cells, nearer 7,000 for generics (some offshore cells as low as 3,000). At about 39% output the top pick spends most of the day idle, which is exactly why TFP says to oversize.

Chlorine demand is estimated at 3 ppm/day for your climate. If you track your daily FC loss (an overnight FC loss test, or your PoolMath logs), entering it makes the output percentages specific to your pool.

advice.text: 1.5″ plumbing holds about 38 GPM on the suction side and 51 GPM on returns before water moves too fast (6 and 8 ft/s). Beyond that you pay in friction, energy and noise — these are efficiency and noise guidelines rather than hard limits, and PVC will carry more if a specific application calls for it — on a new build, going to 2″ now is the cheapest performance decision you will ever make.
